claim: Aldehydes are an integral part of carbon metabolism, energy generation, and signalling pathways in plant physiology.
source: Aldehydes, being an integral part of carbon metabolism, energy generation, and signalling pathways, are ingrained in plant physiology.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general statement about aldehydes in plants.

claim: Land plants have developed intricate metabolic pathways which involve production of reactive aldehydes and its detoxification to survive harsh terrestrial environments.
source: Land plants have developed intricate metabolic pathways which involve production of reactive aldehydes and its detoxification to survive harsh terrestrial environments.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general claim about land plant adaptation.

claim: Physiologically produced aldehydes (formaldehyde, methylglyoxal, and acetaldehyde) generate adducts with aminoacyl-tRNAs.
source: Here, we show that physiologically produced aldehydes, i.e., formaldehyde and methylglyoxal in addition to acetaldehyde, generate adducts with aminoacyl-tRNAs, a substrate for protein synthesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and mass spectrometry results.

claim: Plants possess two distinct chiral proofreading systems, DTD1 and DTD2, of bacterial and archaeal origins, respectively.
source: Plants are unique in possessing two distinct chiral proofreading systems, D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase1 (DTD1) and DTD2, of bacterial and archaeal origins, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Only archaeal DTD2 can remove the stable D-aminoacyl adducts on tRNA.
source: Extensive biochemical analysis revealed that only archaeal DTD2 can remove the stable D-aminoacyl adducts on tRNA thereby shielding archaea and plants from these system-generated aldehydes.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: Loss of DTD2 gene renders plants susceptible to toxic aldehydes.
source: Using Arabidopsis as a model system, we have shown that the loss of DTD2 gene renders plants susceptible to these toxic aldehydes as they generate stable alkyl modification on D-aminoacyl-tRNAs, which are recycled only by DTD2.
evidence: This is supported by toxicity assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: The expansion of aldehyde metabolising repertoire in land plant ancestors strongly correlates with the recruitment of archaeal DTD2.
source: Bioinformatic analysis identifies the expansion of aldehyde metabolising repertoire in land plant ancestors which strongly correlates with the recruitment of archaeal DTD2.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Overexpression of DTD2 offers better protection against aldehydes than in wild type Arabidopsis.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that the overexpression of DTD2 offers better protection against aldehydes than in wild type Arabidopsis highlighting its role as a multi-aldehyde detoxifier that can be explored as a transgenic crop development strategy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Formaldehyde is produced as a by-product of oxidative demethylation by various enzymes.
source: Formaldehyde integrates various carbon metabolic pathways and is produced as a by-product of oxidative demethylation by various enzymes (Jardine et al., 2017; Song et al., 2013; Trézl et al., 1998; Loenarz and Schofield, 2008; Shi et al., 2004; Walport et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Acetaldehyde is an intermediate of anaerobic fermentation.
source: whereas acetaldehyde is an intermediate of anaerobic fermentation (Tadege and Kuhlemeier, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Methylglyoxal is produced via the glycolysis pathway from dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, oxidative deamination of glycine and threonine, fatty acid degradation, and auto-oxidation of glucose inside the cell.
source: Alternatively, MG is produced via the glycolysis pathway from dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, oxidative deamination of glycine and threonine, fatty acid degradation, and auto-oxidation of glucose inside the cell (Mostofa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Aldehydes are involved in carbon metabolism, energy generation, and signalling in all domains of life.
source: These aldehydes are involved in carbon metabolism (Jardine et al., 2017; Song et al., 2013; Trézl et al., 1998; Burgos-Barragan et al., 2017; Hill et al., 2011), energy generation (Tadege and Kuhlemeier, 1997), and signalling (Mostofa et al., 2018; Kosmachevskaya et al., 2017), respectively, in all domains of life.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Plants produce a wide range of aldehydes under various biotic and abiotic stresses.
source: In addition to the three aldehydes discussed above, plants also produce a wide range of other aldehydes under various biotic and abiotic stresses (Mostofa et al., 2018; Jardine et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Aldehydes become genotoxic and cellular hazards at higher concentrations as they irreversibly modify the free amino group of various essential biological macromolecules like nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, and amino acids.
source: Despite their physiological importance, these aldehydes become genotoxic and cellular hazards at higher concentrations as they irreversibly modify the free amino group of various essential biological macromolecules like nucleic acids, proteins, lipids, and amino acids (Seitz and Stickel, 2007; Fang and Vaca, 1997; Matsuda et al., 1999; Fang and Vaca, 1995; Carlsson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Increased levels of formaldehyde and methylglyoxal lead to toxicity in bacteria and mammals.
source: Increased levels of formaldehyde and MG lead to toxicity in various life forms like bacteria (Chen et al., 2016) and mammals (Burgos-Barragan et al., 2017; Pontel et al., 2015; Allaman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Archaea and plants possess aldehydes in high amounts (>25-fold higher than other organisms) yet there is no evidence of toxicity.
source: However, archaea and plants possess these aldehydes in high amounts (>25-fold) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), yet there is no evidence of toxicity (Trézl et al., 1998; Miller et al., 2017; Dingler et al., 2020; Li et al., 2017; Kimmerer and Macdonald, 1987; Quintanilla et al., 2007; Yadav et al., 2005; Rabbani and Thornalley, 2014; Wang et al., 2019; Baskaran et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both archaea and plants have evolved specialised protective mechanisms against toxic aldehyde flux.
source: This suggests that both archaea and plants have evolved specialised protective mechanisms against toxic aldehyde flux.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that archaea and plants tolerate high aldehyde levels.

claim: GEK1 gene is essential for the protection of plants from ethanol and acetaldehyde.
source: Using genetic screening Takashi et al. have identified a gene, called GEK1 at that time, essential for the protection of plants from ethanol and acetaldehyde (Fujishige et al., 2004; Hirayama et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GEK1 was identified to be a homolog of archaeal D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase (DTD).
source: Later, using biochemical and bioinformatic analysis, GEK1 was identified to be a homolog of archaeal D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase (DTD) (Wydau et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: DTDs are trans acting, chiral proofreading enzymes involved in translation quality control and remove D-amino acids mischarged onto tRNAs.
source: DTDs are trans acting, chiral proofreading enzymes involved in translation quality control and remove D-amino acids mischarged onto tRNAs (Calendar and Berg, 1967; Soutourina et al., 1999; Soutourina et al., 2000; Kuncha et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: DTD1 is present in bacteria and eukaryotes, DTD2 in land plants and archaea, and DTD3 in cyanobacteria.
source: DTD function is conserved across all life forms where DTD1 is present in bacteria and eukaryotes, DTD2 in land plants and archaea (Wydau et al., 2007; Ferri-Fioni et al., 2006), and DTD3 in cyanobacteria (Wydau et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: All DTDs are important in protecting organisms from D-amino acids.
source: All DTDs are shown to be important in protecting organisms from D-amino acids (Wydau et al., 2007; Calendar and Berg, 1967; Soutourina et al., 2000; Ferri-Fioni et al., 2006; Wydau et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: DTD2 was found to be involved in protecting plants against ethanol and acetaldehyde.
source: In addition, DTD2 was also found to be involved in protecting plants against ethanol and acetaldehyde (Fujishige et al., 2004; Hirayama et al., 2004; Wydau et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Archaea-derived DTD2 gene alleviates acetaldehyde stress in addition to resolving organellar incompatibility of bacteria-derived DTD1 in land plants.
source: Recently, we identified the biochemical role of archaea-derived DTD2 gene in alleviating acetaldehyde stress in addition to resolving organellar incompatibility of bacteria-derived DTD1 in land plants (Mazeed et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Acetaldehyde irreversibly modifies D-aminoacyl-tRNAs and only DTD2 can recycle the modified D-aa-tRNAs.
source: We have shown that acetaldehyde irreversibly modifies D-aminoacyl-tRNAs (D-aa-tRNA) and only DTD2 can recycle the modified D-aa-tRNAs thus replenishing the free tRNA pool for further translation (Mazeed et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Aldehydes modified aa-tRNAs irrespective of amino acid chirality.
source: We observed that aldehydes modified aa-tRNAs irrespective of amino acid chirality (Figure 1A–G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TLC and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The mass change from formaldehyde, propionaldehyde, butyraldehyde, and MG modification corresponds to a methyl, propyl, butyl, and acetonyl group, respectively.
source: The mass change from formaldehyde, propionaldehyde, butyraldehyde, and MG modification corresponds to a methyl, propyl, butyl, and acetonyl group, respectively (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C-G.

claim: All aldehydes selectively modify only the amino group of amino acids in D-aa-tRNAs.
source: Tandem fragmentation (MS2) of aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs showed that all the aldehydes selectively modify only the amino group of amino acids in D-aa-tRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by MS2 data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-G.

claim: The propensity of modification decreased with increase in the aldehyde chain length with no detectable modification on decanal-treated aa-tRNAs.
source: Interestingly, upon a comparison of modification strength, the propensity of modification decreased with increase in the aldehyde chain length with no detectable modification on decanal-treated aa-tRNAs (Figure 1A and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 1A and H.

claim: The electrophilicity of saturated aldehydes decreases with the increasing chain length of aldehyde.
source: The electrophilicity of saturated aldehydes decreases with the increasing chain length of aldehyde (LoPachin and Gavin, 2014; Pratihar, 2014), thereby reducing modification propensity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The modification propensity of MG is much higher than propionaldehyde due to the high electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon.
source: Exceptionally, the modification propensity of MG is much higher than propionaldehyde (Figure 1H) which is also a three-carbon system (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) and it is likely due to the high electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon (LoPachin and Gavin, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1H and a citation.

claim: The aldehydes with higher propensity of modification are present in higher amounts in plants and archaea.
source: Also, the aldehydes with higher propensity of modification are present in higher amounts in plants and archaea (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Aldehyde modification stabilised the ester linkage by ~13-fold when compared with unmodified aa-tRNA.
source: Strikingly, even the smallest aldehyde modification stabilised the ester linkage by ~13-fold when compared with unmodified aa-tRNA (Figure 1I–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by alkali treatment data shown in Figure 1I-J.

claim: EF-Tu protects L-aa-tRNAs from acetaldehyde modification.
source: Elongation factor thermo unstable (EF-Tu) is shown to protect L-aa-tRNAs from acetaldehyde modification (Mazeed et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The side chain of amino acid in the amino acid binding site of EF-Tu is projected outside.
source: We analysed the aa-tRNA-bound elongation factor structure from bacteria (PDB ids: 1TTT) and found that the side chain of amino acid in the amino acid binding site of EF-Tu is projected outside (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The amino group of amino acid is tightly selected by the main chain atoms of elongation factor thereby lacking a space for aldehydes to enter and then modify the L-aa-tRNAs and Gly-tRNAs.
source: In addition, the amino group of amino acid is tightly selected by the main chain atoms of elongation factor thereby lacking a space for aldehydes to enter and then modify the L-aa-tRNAs and Gly-tRNAs (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Modelling of D-amino acid in the amino acid binding site of EF-Tu shows serious clashes with main chain atoms of EF-Tu, indicating a D-chiral rejection during aa-tRNA binding by elongation factor.
source: Modelling of D-amino acid (either D-phenylalanine or smallest chiral amino acid, D-alanine) in the same site shows serious clashes with main chain atoms of EF-Tu, indicating a D-chiral rejection during aa-tRNA binding by elongation factor (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular modeling shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Elongation factor binds tRNA in a similar way across bacteria and mammals.
source: Next, we superimposed the tRNA-bound mammalian (from Oryctolagus cuniculus) eEF-1A cryoEM structure (PDB id: 5LZS) with bacterial structure to understand the structural differences in terms of tRNA binding and found that elongation factor binds tRNA in a similar way (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Modelling of D-alanine in the amino acid binding site of eEF-1A shows serious clashes with main chain atoms, indicating a general theme of D-chiral rejection during aa-tRNA binding by elongation factor.
source: Modelling of D-alanine in the amino acid binding site of eEF-1A also shows serious clashes with main chain atoms, indicating a general theme of D-chiral rejection during aa-tRNA binding by elongation factor (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular modeling shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Structure-based sequence alignment of elongation factor from bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes shows a strict conservation of amino acid binding site.
source: Structure-based sequence alignment of elongation factor from bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes (both plants and mammals) shows a strict conservation of amino acid binding site (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Activated EF-Tu protected L-aa-tRNAs from formaldehyde.
source: It has been seen that activated EF-Tu protected L-aa-tRNAs from smallest aldehyde suggesting that EF-Tu is a dedicated protector of L-aa-tRNAs from all the cellular metabolites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by TLC data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The lower affinity of D-aa-tRNAs with EF-Tu results in their modification under aldehyde flux.
source: However, the lower affinity of D-aa-tRNAs with EF-Tu results in their modification under aldehyde flux.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Accumulation of stable aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs will deplete the free tRNA pool for translation.
source: Accumulation of these stable aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs will deplete the free tRNA pool for translation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stability of aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs.

claim: Removal of aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs is essential for cell survival.
source: Therefore, removal of aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs is essential for cell survival.
evidence: This is an inference based on the depletion of free tRNA pool.

claim: DTD2 cleaved majority of aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs at 50 pM to 500 nM range.
source: DTD2 cleaved majority of aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs at 50 pM to 500 nM range (Figure 3A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by deacylation assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: DTD2's activity decreases with increase in aldehyde chain lengths.
source: Interestingly, DTD2's activity decreases with increase in aldehyde chain lengths (Figure 3A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by deacylation assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: DTD2 from archaea recycled short chain aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNA adducts.
source: DTD2 from archaea recycled short chain aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNA adducts as expected (Figure 3E–G)
evidence: This claim is supported by deacylation assay data shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: Archaeal DTD2 did not act on aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs longer than three carbons.
source: and, like DTD2 from plants, it did not act on aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs longer than three carbons (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by deacylation assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: DTD1 from plants was inactive on all aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs.
source: Whereas the canonical chiral proofreader, DTD1, from plants was inactive on all aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs (Figure 3I–L and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by deacylation assay data shown in Figure 3I-L.

claim: DTD2 was inactive on butyraldehyde and higher chain length aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs.
source: Interestingly, DTD2 was inactive on butyraldehyde, and higher chain length aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs (Figure 3D and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2J–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by deacylation assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: DTD2 exerts its protection till propionaldehyde with a significant preference for methylglyoxal and formaldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs.
source: This suggests that DTD2 exerts its protection till propionaldehyde with a significant preference for methylglyoxal and formaldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the deacylation assay data.

claim: The physiological levels of higher chain length aldehydes are comparatively much lesser in plants and archaea.
source: It is worth noting that the physiological levels of higher chain length aldehydes are comparatively much lesser in plants and archaea (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), indicating the coevolution of DTD2 activity with the presence of toxic aldehydes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and represents an inference about coevolution.

claim: DTD2 showed ~100-fold higher activity on MG-modified D-aa-tRNAs compared to propionaldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs.
source: Even though both MG and propionaldehyde generate a three-carbon chain modification, DTD2 showed ~100-fold higher activity on MG-modified D-aa-tRNAs (Figure 3B–C, F–G, and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by deacylation assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Peptidyl-tRNA hydrolase (PTH) was inactive on formaldehyde and MG-modified L- and D-aa-tRNAs.
source: It is interesting to note that peptidyl-tRNA hydrolase (PTH), which recycles on N-acetyl/peptidyl-L-aa-tRNAs and has a similar fold to DTD2, was inactive on formaldehyde and MG-modified L- and D-aa-tRNAs (Figure 3M and Figure 3—figure supplement 2M–Q).
evidence: This claim is supported by deacylation assay data shown in Figure 3M and Figure 3—figure supplement 2M-Q.

claim: DTD2 is the only aldehyde detoxifier recycling the tRNA pool in both plants and archaea.
source: Overall, our biochemical assays with multiple trans acting proofreaders (DTD1 and DTD2) and peptidyl-tRNA recycling enzymes (both bacterial and archaeal PTH) suggest that DTD2 is the only aldehyde detoxifier recycling the tRNA pool in both plants and archaea.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biochemical assay data comparing DTD1, DTD2, and PTH activities.

claim: dtd2 plants were susceptible to ethanol.
source: Similar to earlier results (Fujishige et al., 2004; Hirayama et al., 2004; Wydau et al., 2007), dtd2-/- (dtd2 hereafter) plants were susceptible to ethanol (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) confirming the non-functionality of DTD2 gene in dtd2 plants.
evidence: This claim is supported by toxicity assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and citations.

claim: dtd2 plants were found to be sensitive to both formaldehyde and MG.
source: These dtd2 plants were found to be sensitive to both formaldehyde and MG (Figure 4B–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by toxicity assay data shown in Figure 4B-G.

claim: The sensitivity of dtd2 plants to aldehydes was alleviated by complementing dtd2 mutant line with genomic copy of wild type DTD2.
source: This sensitivity was alleviated by complementing dtd2 mutant line with genomic copy of wild type DTD2 (Figure 4A–G), indicating that DTD2-mediated detoxification plays an important role in plant aldehyde stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 4A-G.

claim: dtd2 plants show a significant reduction (~40%) in germination.
source: As expected, dtd2 plants show a significant reduction (~40%) in germination (Figure 4H–I) and this effect was reversed in the DTD2 rescue line (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by germination assay data shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: The toxic effects of formaldehyde and MG were enhanced upon D-amino acid supplementation.
source: Interestingly, these toxic effects (on both growth and germination) of formaldehyde and MG were enhanced upon D-amino acid supplementation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by toxicity assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DTD2's chiral proofreading activity is associated with aldehyde stress removal activity.
source: These observations suggest that DTD2's chiral proofreading activity is associated with aldehyde stress removal activity as well.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enhanced toxicity with D-amino acid supplementation.

claim: The catalytic mutant line showed a similar phenotype as dtd2 plants under aldehyde stress, confirming the role of DTD2's biochemical activity in relieving general aldehyde toxicity in plants.
source: The catalytic mutant line showed a similar phenotype as dtd2 plants under aldehyde stress (Figure 4A–I), confirming the role of DTD2's biochemical activity in relieving general aldehyde toxicity in plants.
evidence: This claim is supported by toxicity assay data with catalytic mutant shown in Figure 4A-I.

claim: Formaldehyde- and MG-modified D-aa-tRNA adducts accumulate in E. coli in the absence of DTD protein.
source: We could identify the accumulation of both formaldehyde- and MG-modified D-aa-tRNA adducts via mass spectrometry (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-H.

claim: DTD2-mediated detoxification protects plants from physiologically abundant toxic aldehydes.
source: Overall, our results show that DTD2-mediated detoxification protects plants from physiologically abundant toxic aldehydes.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the in vivo and biochemical data.

claim: The DTD2 overexpression line was more tolerant to both formaldehyde and MG when compared with wild type.
source: Strikingly, we found that the DTD2 overexpression line was more tolerant to both the aldehydes (formaldehyde and MG) when compared with wild type (Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by toxicity assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: DTD2 overexpression resulted in >50% increased seedling growth when compared with that of wild type.
source: DTD2 overexpression resulted in >50% increased seedling growth when compared with that of wild type (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The growth difference was more pronounced when D-amino acids were supplemented with varying concentrations of aldehydes.
source: The growth difference was more pronounced when D-amino acids were supplemented with varying concentrations of aldehydes (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: DTD2 overexpression plants showed extensive root growth under the influence of both formaldehyde and MG.
source: Interestingly, DTD2 overexpression plants showed extensive root growth under the influence of both formaldehyde and MG (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by root growth data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Plants produce aldehydes in huge amounts under various stress conditions.
source: Plants produce these aldehydes in huge amounts under various stress conditions (Jardine et al., 2009; Yadav et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Plant tolerance to various abiotic stresses is strongly influenced by root growth.
source: and plant tolerance to various abiotic stresses is strongly influenced by root growth (Seo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The enhanced root growth by DTD2 overexpression under aldehyde stress implies that DTD2 overexpression offers a viable method to generate multi-stress-resistant crop varieties.
source: The enhanced root growth by DTD2 overexpression under aldehyde stress implies that DTD2 overexpression offers a viable method to generate multi-stress-resistant crop varieties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the root growth data and knowledge about stress tolerance.

claim: DTD2 from charophyte algae Klebsormedium nitens recycled aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs adducts like other plant and archaeal DTD2s.
source: Therefore, we checked the biochemical activity of DTD2 from a charophyte algae, Klebsormedium nitens (Kn), and found that it also recycled aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs adducts like other plant and archaeal DTD2s (Figure 6A–C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by deacylation assay data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: The multi-aldehyde problem in plants has its roots in their distant ancestors, charophytes.
source: This suggests that the multi-aldehyde problem in plants has its roots in their distant ancestors, charophytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the activity of charophyte DTD2.

claim: Land plants encode greater number of ALDH genes compared to green algae.
source: Multiple bioinformatic analyses have shown that land plants encode greater number of ALDH genes compared to green algae (Tola et al., 2020; Islam and Ghosh, 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Glyoxalase family (GlyI, GlyII, and GlyIII) has expanded exclusively in streptophytic plants.
source: and glyoxalase family (GlyI, GlyII, and GlyIII), known to clear MG, has expanded exclusively in streptophytic plants (Singla-Pareek et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Land plants encode greater number of AOX genes in addition to ALDH genes compared to green algae.
source: We identified that land plants also encode greater number of AOX genes in addition to ALDH genes compared to green algae (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Formaldehyde is involved in 5 pathways, 60 enzymes, and 94 KEGG reactions.
source: A search for the formaldehyde (C00067) and MG (C00546) in KEGG database (Kanehisa et al., 2016) has shown that formaldehyde is involved in 5 pathways, 60 enzymes, and 94 KEGG reactions
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG database search.

claim: Methylglyoxal is involved in 6 pathways, 16 enzymes, and 16 KEGG reactions.
source: while MG in 6 pathways, 16 enzymes, and 16 KEGG reactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by KEGG database search.

claim: Plants encode majority of the genes related for formaldehyde and MG and they are conserved throughout land plants.
source: Strikingly, we found that plants encode majority of the genes related for formaldehyde and MG and they are conserved throughout land plants (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–G) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 6D and supplementary data.

claim: Plants produce significant amounts of formaldehyde while reshuffling pectin in their cell wall during cell division, development, and tissue damage.
source: Plants produce significant amounts of formaldehyde while reshuffling pectin in their cell wall during cell division, development, and tissue damage (Wu et al., 2018; Dorokhov et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Plants contain ~33% pectin in their cell walls that provides strength and flexibility.
source: Plants contain ~33% pectin in their cell walls that provides strength and flexibility (Jarvis et al., 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Pectin biosynthesis and degradation is a land plant-specific adaptation that originated in early diverging streptophytic algae.
source: When checked for the presence of genes responsible for the pectin biosynthesis and degradation, we identified that it is a land plant-specific adaptation that originated in early diverging streptophytic algae (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: There is an expansion of aldehyde metabolising repertoire in land plants and their ancestors indicating the sudden aldehyde burst accompanying terrestrialisation which strongly correlates with the recruitment of DTD2.
source: Overall, our bioinformatic analysis in addition to earlier studies has identified an expansion of aldehyde metabolising repertoire in land plants and their ancestors indicating the sudden aldehyde burst accompanying terrestrialisation which strongly correlates with the recruitment of DTD2 (Figure 6E and Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on bioinformatic analysis and earlier studies.

claim: Aldehydes with higher reactivity (formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, and MG) are present in higher amounts in plants and archaea and DTD2 provides modified-D-aa-tRNA deacylase activity against these aldehydes.
source: Through this work, we find a correlation between physiological abundance of various aldehydes, their modification propensity, and DTD2's aldehyde protection range. Aldehydes with higher reactivity (formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, and MG) are present in higher amounts in plants and archaea and DTD2 provides modified-D-aa-tRNA deacylase activity against these aldehydes.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the data presented.

claim: DTD2's biochemical activity decreases with increase in the aldehyde chain length.
source: DTD2's biochemical activity decreases with increase in the aldehyde chain length.
evidence: This is supported by the deacylation assay data in Figure 3.

claim: The absence of carbonyl carbon in the propionaldehyde-modified substrate and DTD2's preferential activity on the bulkier MG-modified substrate points to a clear evolutionary selection pressure for the abundant and physiologically relevant aldehyde.
source: The absence of carbonyl carbon in the propionaldehyde-modified substrate and DTD2's preferential activity on the bulkier MG-modified substrate points to a clear evolutionary selection pressure for the abundant and physiologically relevant aldehyde.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biochemical activity data and substrate structure.

claim: All PTH substrates contain carbonyl carbon at the alpha position after the amino group of amino acid in L-aa-tRNA.
source: In total contrast to DTD2, all PTH substrates contain carbonyl carbon at the alpha position after the amino group of amino acid in L-aa-tRNA (Atherly, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The inactivity of PTH on MG-modified L- and D-aa-tRNAs suggests its specificity for carbonyl carbon at alpha position.
source: The inactivity of PTH on MG-modified L- and D-aa-tRNAs suggests its specificity for carbonyl carbon at alpha position (Figure 3—figure supplement 2Q).
evidence: This is an inference based on the PTH activity data and substrate structure.

claim: The sensitivity of dtd2 plants to aldehydes of higher prevalence and hyper-propensity for modification indicates the physiological coevolution of aldehyde phytochemistry and recruitment of DTD2 in land plants.
source: The sensitivity of dtd2 plants to aldehydes of higher prevalence and hyper-propensity for modification indicates the physiological coevolution of aldehyde phytochemistry and recruitment of DTD2 in land plants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vivo toxicity data and aldehyde abundance.

claim: Plants are being used as air purifiers as they act as aldehyde scavengers from the environment.
source: Despite the toxic effects of reactive aldehydes, plants are being used as air purifiers as they act as aldehyde scavengers from the environment (Teiri et al., 2018; Aydogan and Montoya, 2011; Wang et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Plants have higher removal rates for formaldehyde and acetaldehyde as compared to other higher chain length aldehydes from the environment.
source: Moreover, plants have higher removal rates for formaldehyde and acetaldehyde as compared to other higher chain length aldehydes from the environment (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of enzymes (PDC, ADH, ALDH, and glyoxalase) involved in aldehyde detoxification are shown to provide multi-stress tolerance.
source: These aldehydes are produced under various biotic and abiotic stresses in plants and overexpression of enzymes (PDC, ADH, ALDH, and glyoxalase) involved in aldehyde detoxification are shown to provide multi-stress tolerance (Gupta et al., 2018; Quimio et al., 2000; Su et al., 2020; Sun, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DTD2 provides multi-aldehyde stress tolerance in the context of detoxifying adducts formed on aa-tRNA.
source: Our in vivo results strongly suggests that DTD2 provides multi-aldehyde stress tolerance in the context of detoxifying adducts formed on aa-tRNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overexpression data.

claim: DTD2 facilitates the release of free tRNA pool thus relieving translation arrest.
source: This facilitates the release of free tRNA pool thus relieving translation arrest.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of DTD2 action.

claim: The role of reactive aldehydes like formaldehyde in the origin of life is inevitable.
source: The role of reactive aldehydes like formaldehyde in the origin of life is inevitable (Kitadai and Maruyama, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The presence of reactive aldehydes and D-amino acids for a long time suggests an ancient origin of DTD2 activity in last archaeal common ancestor.
source: The presence of reactive aldehydes (Miller and Urey, 1959; Miller, 1957) and D-amino acids (Parker et al., 2011; Naraoka et al., 2023) for such a long time suggests an ancient origin of DTD2 activity in last archaeal common ancestor.
evidence: This is an inference based on citations about ancient presence of aldehydes and D-amino acids.

claim: Archaea secrete enormous amount of formaldehyde into the environment as they grow.
source: As archaea thrive in extreme conditions, they secrete enormous amount of formaldehyde into the environment as they grow (Moran et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: DTD2 from archaea can efficiently recycle physiologically abundant toxic aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs like plant DTD2s.
source: We have shown that DTD2 from archaea can efficiently recycle physiologically abundant toxic aldehyde-modified D-aa-tRNAs like plant DTD2s.
evidence: This is supported by the biochemical data in Figure 3.

claim: The adduct removal activity was utilised by the archaeal domain as they produce more aldehydes and thrive in harsh environments and it was later acquired by plants.
source: The adduct removal activity was utilised by the archaeal domain as they produce more aldehydes and thrive in harsh environments (Gribaldo and Brochier-Armanet, 2006; Merino et al., 2019; Spang et al., 2017) and it was later acquired by plants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of DTD2 and citations about archaeal environments.

claim: Bog ecosystems are highly anaerobic, rich in D-amino acids and ammonia, which lead to enhanced production of aldehydes in their inhabitants.
source: Bog ecosystems, earlier proposed site for DTD2 gene transfer (Mazeed et al., 2021), are highly anaerobic, rich in D-amino acids and ammonia (Taffner et al., 2018; Vranova et al., 2012; Kharanzhevskaya et al., 2011), which lead to enhanced production of aldehydes (acetaldehyde [Tadege and Kuhlemeier, 1997] and MG Borysiuk et al., 2018) in their inhabitants.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Recruitment of archaeal DTD2 by a land plant ancestor must have aided in the terrestrialisation of early land plants.
source: Thus, recruitment of archaeal DTD2 by a land plant ancestor must have aided in the terrestrialisation of early land plants.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between DTD2 recruitment and aldehyde metabolism expansion.

claim: There are no common incidences of archaeal gene transfer to eukaryotes.
source: Considering the fact that there are no common incidences of archaeal gene transfer to eukaryotes, it is unclear whether the DTD2 gene was transferred directly to land plant ancestor from archaea or perhaps was mediated by an unidentified intermediate bacterium warrants further investigation.
evidence: This is stated as a fact with speculation about the mechanism of gene transfer.

claim: The study has established the role of archaeal origin DTD2 in land plants by mitigating the toxicity induced by aldehydes during protein biosynthesis.
source: Overall, the study has established the role of archaeal origin DTD2 in land plants by mitigating the toxicity induced by aldehydes during protein biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the overall findings.
